as_told: A large supermarket chain mined its checkout data and found that men who bought diapers, often on Thursday or Friday evenings, also bought beer. Nobody would have guessed this. The store moved the beer next to the diapers and sales of both went up.
lesson: Mining sales data finds surprising buying patterns that a retailer can turn into profit.
what_happened: Teradata, a division of NCR, said in an August 2002 press release that ten years earlier it had looked at a retailer's sales data and found that beer and diapers were often bought together in the evening hours. The release does not name the retailer, does not say the buyers were men, and does not claim that the retailer acted on the finding. According to D. J. Power (2002), Thomas Blischok, who led the study for Osco Drug stores, said in a Teradata webcast that the retailer never did anything with the relationship; this reaches us only as Power's quotation. I found no record of any shelf change or sales gain.

earliest_telling.where: Data Mining (technology note for Management 274A, Anderson Graduate School of Management, UCLA, Spring 1996; copyright June 1996), page 'What is Data Mining?'
earliest_telling.quote: For example, one Midwest grocery chain used the data mining capacity of Oracle software to analyze local buying patterns. They discovered that when men bought diapers on Thursdays and Saturdays, they also tended to buy beer.

original.what: NCR Teradata Division press release 'Teradata takes data mining beyond beer & diapers', Dayton, Ohio, as published by Scoop (New Zealand) on 5 August 2002
original.quote: pioneered the field of data mining by looking at sales data from a retailer and discovering that in the evening hours, beer and diapers are often purchased together.

lesson_verdict.why: I found no controlled study showing that acting on a surprising association found by mining sales data produced a measured profit. Retail data-mining researchers wrote in 2001 that retailers found it hard to turn association rules into concrete marketing decisions.

source.what: Brijs, Goethals, Swinnen, Vanhoof and Wets, 'A Data Mining Framework for Optimal Product Selection in Retail Supermarket Data: The Generalized PROFSET Model', arXiv:cs/0112013 (2001)
source.quote: Still, retailers often complain about how to adopt association rules to optimize concrete retail marketing-mix decisions.

search_steps: Open Library full-text search for "beer and diapers": 247 hits; the earliest relevant books are from 1997 (SPIE proceedings of a 21 November 1996 conference; Simon, Data Warehousing for Dummies). These are lending-only scans; full text could not be downloaded (HTTP 401), so they are not quoted.
Open Library full-text search for "diapers and beer": 194 hits; earliest relevant is Berry and Linoff, Data Mining Techniques (1997), with a Thursday rule. Lending-only, not quoted.
Google Books API search: refused with HTTP 429 (daily quota), so I stopped and did not retry.

D. J. Power, DSS News vol. 3 no. 23 (10 November 2002), 'Ask Dan! What is the true story about data mining, beer and diapers?': the live page now fails; saved the 24 October 2004 Wayback copy. It quotes a Financial Times article of 7 February 1996 (not online in full text; not quoted), Bill Palace's UCLA notes of Spring 1996, and Blischok's 2002 webcast.

Followed Power to Bill Palace's UCLA notes; saved the 1999 Wayback copy of the page and of its index page, which gives 'Spring 1996' and 'Copyright June, 1996'. This is the earliest telling I could save, and it names men.
Power also quotes John Earle (1998 web note) and Tom Fawcett (KDnuggets 2000, third-hand) saying Blischok blurred hypotheses and findings; these are relayed and used only as leads.
Searched the web for a 1992-1995 newspaper or trade-press telling and for the Teradata webcast transcript itself; found neither online.

Followed Power to Ronny Kohavi's ICML-98 slides 'Crossing the Chasm' (chasm.pdf); saved the Wayback copy. Slide 22 says K. Heath in Blischok's group ran SQL self joins in 1990 over data of 50 stores and 90 days, and that the pattern was 'Unlikely to be significant'. This is Kohavi's report of what Heath told him, so it is a lead only.

Power quotes Blischok from a Teradata transcript of the 31 July 2002 webcast: 'we did discover that between 5:00 and 7:00 p.m. that consumers bought beer and diapers' and 'in reality they never did anything with beer and diapers relationships'. These are relayed words in Power's text, so they are leads, not evidence.

Searched for Teradata's own copy of the webcast or transcript: found NCR media advisories of July 2002 on investor.ncr.com, but the site refused automated download (Access Denied). Found and saved Teradata's 5 August 2002 press release as republished by Scoop.

Searched for a field study of acting on association rules: a 2020 SMU conference paper (Cheong and Chia) could not be downloaded (both hosts blocked automated access). Saved Brijs et al. 2001 (arXiv) as the lesson source.
confidence_note: Teradata's own release supports that some beer-and-diapers affinity was found, but not the men, the shelf move or the profit. If Blischok's words as quoted by Power were accepted as his own, the class would be 'changed' (a real finding that was never acted on). Blischok's own staff (John Earle, via Power) said he mixed tested findings with hypotheses. Earlier tellings (Financial Times 1996, trade press 1992-1995) may exist but were not online.
